title: Accounting Foundations
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Accounting is the language of business — it records, classifies, and reports economic activity. The Accounting Equation is inviolable: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Every transaction affects at least two accounts (double-entry bookkeeping), keeping the equation balanced. Debits increase assets and expenses; credits increase liabilities, equity, and revenue. Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred (not when cash moves); cash accounting records when cash moves. GAAP/IFRS are the rule frameworks ensuring comparability.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A company buys $10,000 of equipment with cash. Assets increase by $10,000 (equipment) and decrease by $10,000 (cash) — the equation stays balanced, and net worth is unchanged. Buying an asset is not an expense; it is a conversion of one asset into another.

PRACTICE: 1) Journal three transactions using debits and credits. 2) Show how each keeps A = L + E balanced. 3) Explain why accrual profit can differ from cash in the bank.
quiz_json: [{"q": "The accounting equation is:", "options": ["Revenue \u2212 Expenses = Profit", "Assets = Liabilities + Equity", "Cash In \u2212 Cash Out = Balance", "Debits = Profits"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "Assets = Liabilities + Equity, always."}, {"q": "Accrual accounting records revenue when:", "options": ["Cash is received", "It is earned", "The invoice is paid", "The year ends"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "Revenue is recorded when earned, not when cash moves."}, {"q": "Buying equipment with cash is:", "options": ["An expense", "A conversion of one asset to another", "A liability", "Revenue"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "Assets shift; net worth is unchanged."}]

title: The Three Financial Statements
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The Income Statement (P&L) shows performance over a period: Revenue − COGS = Gross Profit; − Operating Expenses = Operating Income (EBIT); − Interest & Taxes = Net Income. The Balance Sheet is a snapshot at a point in time: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. The Cash Flow Statement reconciles net income to actual cash across three sections: Operating, Investing, Financing. The statements interlock: net income flows to retained earnings on the balance sheet and starts the cash flow statement.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A company reports $1M net income but has negative cash flow — because $1.5M was tied up in growing receivables. Profitable companies go bankrupt from cash starvation. This is why the cash flow statement exists: profit is an opinion, cash is a fact.

PRACTICE: 1) Build a simple P&L from revenue and cost data. 2) Show how net income links all three statements. 3) Identify a case where profit and cash flow diverge.

title: Recording & the Accounting Cycle
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The cycle: transactions → journal entries → general ledger → trial balance → adjusting entries → financial statements → closing entries. Adjusting entries capture accruals (revenue earned but not billed), deferrals (cash received before earned), depreciation, and accrued expenses. The trial balance proves debits equal credits but does NOT prove correctness — a transaction posted to the wrong account still balances. Closing entries zero out temporary accounts (revenue, expenses) into retained earnings.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A company receives $12,000 in December for a year of service starting January. Cash increases $12,000, but revenue is zero — the offset is Deferred Revenue, a liability. Each month, $1,000 moves from liability to revenue as it's earned. Recognizing it all in December would overstate the year's profit fourfold.

PRACTICE: 1) Write adjusting entries for accrued salary and prepaid rent. 2) Build a trial balance. 3) Explain why a balanced trial balance can still be wrong.

title: Financial Statement Analysis
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Ratios turn statements into insight. Liquidity: Current Ratio (Current Assets/Current Liabilities), Quick Ratio (excludes inventory). Profitability: Gross Margin, Operating Margin, Net Margin, Return on Equity (ROE = Net Income/Equity), Return on Assets. Efficiency: Inventory Turnover, Days Sales Outstanding (DSO), Asset Turnover. Leverage: Debt-to-Equity, Interest Coverage (EBIT/Interest). DuPont decomposition: ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier — revealing whether returns come from profitability, efficiency, or leverage.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Two firms both show 20% ROE. DuPont reveals Firm A earns it from 15% net margins; Firm B from 5x leverage on thin margins. Identical headline number, radically different risk. Ratios without decomposition mislead.

PRACTICE: 1) Compute liquidity, profitability, and leverage ratios for a company. 2) Decompose ROE using DuPont. 3) Explain what a rising DSO signals about collections.

title: Managerial & Cost Accounting
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Financial accounting reports outward; managerial accounting informs internal decisions. Cost behavior: fixed (rent), variable (materials), mixed. Contribution Margin = Price − Variable Cost; it funds fixed costs and profit. Break-even units = Fixed Costs / Contribution Margin per unit. Activity-Based Costing (ABC) assigns overhead by actual activity drivers, exposing which products truly lose money. Sunk costs are irrelevant to decisions; only incremental costs matter.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A product sells for $50 with $30 variable cost — contribution margin $20. Fixed costs are $200,000. Break-even = 200,000/20 = 10,000 units. Below that, every sale still helps (it covers some fixed cost) as long as price exceeds variable cost — a crucial insight often missed when firms kill products that appear 'unprofitable' under full-cost allocation.

PRACTICE: 1) Calculate break-even units for a product. 2) Decide whether to accept a special order priced below full cost. 3) Identify a sunk cost you'd be tempted to consider.

title: Advanced Topics: Valuation, Taxes & Consolidation
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Deferred tax arises when book and tax treatments differ (e.g., depreciation methods). Inventory methods: FIFO, LIFO, Weighted Average — each produces different profit under inflation (FIFO shows higher profit; LIFO lower and lower taxes). Depreciation methods: straight-line vs accelerated affect earnings timing, not total. Consolidation combines parent and subsidiary, eliminating intercompany transactions. Goodwill arises when purchase price exceeds fair value of net assets — and is tested annually for impairment, never amortized under current standards.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Under rising prices, LIFO charges the newest (higher) costs to COGS, lowering reported profit and taxes. FIFO does the opposite. Identical physical inventory, different reported earnings — proving that accounting policy choice materially shapes the picture without any change in reality.

PRACTICE: 1) Compare FIFO vs LIFO profit under inflation. 2) Explain how goodwill arises in an acquisition. 3) Identify a source of deferred tax liability.

title: Grandmaster — Controls, Audit & Earnings Quality
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Internal controls prevent and detect error and fraud — segregation of duties is the core principle (whoever authorizes shouldn't also record and custody). The Fraud Triangle: pressure, opportunity, rationalization — remove any one and fraud is far less likely. Audit provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance. Earnings quality: high-quality earnings are cash-backed and repeatable; red flags include growing gap between net income and operating cash flow, aggressive revenue recognition, and repeated 'one-time' charges. Accruals are where manipulation hides.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A company's net income rises 20% while operating cash flow falls. The gap is a widening receivables balance — revenue booked but not collected. This divergence is the single most reliable early warning of aggressive or fraudulent revenue recognition; it preceded most major accounting scandals.

PRACTICE: 1) Design segregation of duties for a cash process. 2) Assess earnings quality using the income-to-cash-flow gap. 3) Identify three red flags in a set of statements.

title: King Level — Accounting as Strategic Intelligence
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At the highest level, accounting is not compliance — it is the instrument panel for capital allocation. The King-level operator reads statements to answer: where is value created, where destroyed, and where should the next dollar go? Economic Value Added (EVA) = NOPAT − (Capital × Cost of Capital) — profit only counts above the cost of the capital consumed. Unit economics (contribution per customer, CAC payback, LTV) matter more than aggregate profit in growth businesses. Accounting choices signal to markets; consistency and conservatism build credibility, while aggressive policy invites discount.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A division shows $2M accounting profit but consumed $30M of capital at a 12% cost — EVA = 2 − 3.6 = −$1.6M. It is destroying value despite looking profitable. This distinction — accounting profit vs economic profit — is why capital gets misallocated for years in companies that only read the P&L.

PRACTICE: 1) Compute EVA for a business unit. 2) Build unit economics for a customer cohort. 3) Recommend where the next $1M of capital should go and defend it with numbers.
